prompt: Explain how the U.S. Supreme Court works using only bass-fishing tournament metaphors. Keep going well past the point where it makes sense.
response:
The U.S. Supreme Court is the final bass-fishing tournament of the American legal system. Nine professional anglers (the justices) sit in a sleek, black bass boat that never touches water. They don’t actually fish. They judge everybody else’s casts.

Every year, thousands of regular fishermen (lower-court cases) compete in local derbies, regional classics, and circuit tournaments. Most of them lose and go home. A few catch enough legal largemouth to earn a ticket to the big show: the Supreme Court Classic, held every term on the marble dock in Washington.

To even get invited, a fisherman has to file a cert petition that looks like a flawless tournament application—perfectly formatted, with a crisp cover page and exactly the right number of supporting affidavits about “federal questions of exceptional importance.” The justices, acting as the tournament committee, vote in secret during their weekly “conference weigh-in.” If four of them raise their hands and say “this one might be a keeper,” the case is granted. That’s called “granting cert.” If they all shrug and say “nah, that fish is barely legal,” the petition sinks to the bottom like a bad crankbait.

Once a case is in the tournament, both sides get to make their final casts. Each lawyer stands at the back of the boat and throws a lure toward the justices, who sit up front in high-backed casting chairs. The lawyers only have thirty minutes. That’s it. No live-well, no culling, no “one more cast.” Oral arguments are pure sight-fishing under brutal pressure. The justices interrupt constantly, firing off trick questions the way tournament pros flip a jig into a brush pile just to see what comes out. Justice Scalia used to skip his lure across the water like a sidewinder; Justice Ginsburg preferred a slow, deadly drop-shot that never moved until the exact right moment.

After the final cast, the boat goes quiet. The justices disappear into the “conference room,” which is really just a luxurious livewell where they argue for hours, sometimes days. No spectators, no cameras, no weigh-master. They vote. The senior justice on the winning side gets to choose who writes the “majority opinion”—the official tournament report that explains why this particular bass was the biggest, baddest, most constitutionally correct fish in the lake.
